entries.name: Origen
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds 16 of his own works on the shelf of the Alexandrian teachers, in Greek, Latin and English. Eusebius gave most of a book of his Church History to Origen's life.
entries.floorNote: His own faith is not in question here. Some of his bolder ideas were attacked long after his death, and a church council condemned them about three centuries later.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within the Alexandrian teachers, whose best-known voice he is. He moved his teaching to Caesarea, and his pupils, readers and critics spread across the churches of the East and West.
entries.why: Origen is the scholar of the early church. He began to teach at Alexandria as a teenager, after his father died a martyr. He wrote on almost every book of the Bible. Late in life he was tortured for his faith, and he died a few years after.
entries.teaser: Alexandria and Caesarea, c. 203 to 253 CE: a martyr's son who became the church's first great Bible scholar, and was argued over for centuries.
entries.longDescription:
His father was beheaded for his faith while Origen was still young. Eusebius says Origen was in his eighteenth year when he took charge of teaching new believers at Alexandria. He wrote commentaries on most of Scripture.

About 231 he left Alexandria for Caesarea in Palestine. His own bishop, Demetrius, cut him off. Students came to him there. Two brothers from Pontus stayed five years and later became bishops at home.

Under the emperor Decius he was thrown into prison. Eusebius tells of chains, an iron collar and the stocks. He survived, but he died soon after, aged sixty-nine.
voices: Origen — commentator, textual scholar and teacher, whose words the Library holds in Greek and Latin
Eusebius of Caesarea — the historian who wrote down Origen's life, and who kept his books at Caesarea
entries.legacy: His books outlived him, and so did the fight over them. Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus drew on his work, and Rufinus put him into Latin. Jerome first used his work and later called his teachings poison. Methodius wrote against his view of the body. Much later, the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria called his books blasphemous.

entries.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds 22 of his own works on the shelf of the Alexandrian teachers. They include his books against the Arians, his defenses and his letters, in Greek, Latin and English.
entries.floorNote: Not in question. He spent his life defending the Creed of Nicaea.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within the Alexandrian teachers, whose shelf holds his works. He was also the first bishop of the church of Alexandria on this map. He fought the party of Arius by name.
entries.why: Athanasius was bishop of Alexandria for forty-five years and was driven out five times. Through all of it he held to the faith stated at Nicaea, where he had gone as a young deacon.
entries.teaser: Alexandria, 328 to 373 CE. A bishop sent into exile five times, who held to the creed of Nicaea and died in his own city.
entries.longDescription:
Two churches claim Athanasius. The Coptic church counts him as its own, and so do the churches that accepted Chalcedon. The Library keeps his works on the shelf of the Alexandrian teachers.

As a young deacon he went with his bishop, Alexander, to the Council of Nicaea in 325. On 8 June 328 he became bishop of Alexandria himself.

Rival bishops and emperors drove him from his city again and again. His editor counts five exiles. Between them he wrote against the Arians, in his Four Discourses and other books.

He died in Alexandria on 2 May 373, in the forty-sixth year of his time as bishop.
voices: Athanasius of Alexandria — bishop for forty-five years, whose defenses, treatises and letters the Library holds
Cyril of Alexandria — a later bishop of the same city, who wrote that he followed 'our blessed and all-celebrated Father Athanasius'
entries.legacy: His own city went on reading him. Around 433 Cyril, a later bishop of Alexandria, wrote that he followed Athanasius and would not depart from him at all. He even sent out true copies of one of Athanasius's letters, because a false version was going round.

entries.name: Gregory of Nyssa
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds 20 of his own works on the shelf of the Cappadocians: his books against Eunomius, his treatises on the soul and on the faith, his letters, and his Life of his sister Macrina.
entries.floorNote: Not in question. He was one of the bishops the emperor named in 381 as a standard of the Nicene faith.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within the Cappadocians, with his brother Basil and their friend Gregory of Nazianzus. He finished Basil's answer to Eunomius and wrote against those who denied the Spirit was God. A hostile party drove him from his see for a time.
entries.why: Gregory was the younger brother of Basil and Macrina, and the boldest thinker of the family. He wrote the long reply to Eunomius that Basil left unfinished. He also wrote the only life we have of his sister.
entries.teaser: Nyssa, 372 to 394 CE: a bishop sent away and brought back, who wrote his sister's life and finished his brother's fight.
entries.longDescription:
Gregory was one of ten children. Basil was the eldest son and Macrina the eldest child. Gregory and his brother Peter both became bishops.

Early in 372 he was chosen bishop of the small town of Nyssa. Two or three years later his enemies brought charges against him, and he was sent away. He came back to his see in 378.

After Basil died, Gregory took up his brother's quarrel with Eunomius. He wrote a long work in reply. In 381 he was at the council in Constantinople.

He also wrote the Life of Macrina. It is the only record of her that survives. The last trace of Gregory himself is a synod at Constantinople in 394.
voices: Gregory of Nyssa — bishop, theologian and his sister's biographer, whose treatises and letters the Library holds
Macrina — his elder sister, known only through the Life he wrote of her
entries.legacy: In July 381 the emperor Theodosius named him in a law. Bishops in Pontus had to be in communion with Gregory of Nyssa, or with Helladius of Caesarea, to count as Catholic. The council of that year gave the two men charge of the church in Pontus.

entries.name: Ephrem the Syrian
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds 11 of his own works on the shelf of the Syriac church of Edessa and Nisibis: hymns, homilies and prose refutations, in Syriac and English.
entries.floorNote: Not in question. He holds the faith the Nicene Creed states.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within the Syriac church of Edessa and Nisibis, as its great hymnwriter. A later teacher of the Church of the East said Ephrem founded a school at Edessa after 363.
entries.why: Ephrem taught the faith in song. He served as a deacon. The sources differ on where he was ordained. His hymns carried the church's teaching in words a whole congregation could sing.
entries.teaser: Nisibis and Edessa, c. 338 to 373 CE: a deacon who sang his city through three sieges, and taught a church its faith in hymns.
entries.longDescription:
Ephrem was born at Nisibis and learned from its bishop, Jacob. He lived through three Persian sieges of the city.

In 363 Rome gave Nisibis up to Persia, and its Christians left. Ephrem settled at Edessa.

He wrote a great deal: sermons, commentaries and hymns. Most writers date his death to 373. Some think he lived until 378.
voices: Ephrem — deacon and hymnwriter, whose hymns and homilies the Library holds
Barhadbeshabba — a later teacher of the Church of the East, who told how Ephrem taught at Edessa
entries.legacy: The Church of the East kept his name as a teacher. Barhadbeshabba wrote about 600. He said Ephrem set up a school at Edessa after Nisibis passed to Persia. He traced his own church's school at Nisibis back through the teachers who came after.

entries.name: John Chrysostom
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Very rich. The Library holds 36 of his own works on the shelf of the Antiochene preachers: hundreds of sermons, treatises and letters. Palladius, a bishop who stood by him, wrote a dialogue on his life.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within the Antiochene preachers, as their best-known voice. The court chose him as bishop of Constantinople. Then two synods condemned him, and the emperor sent him away. Calvin and the Lutherans quoted him a thousand years later.
entries.why: John preached at Antioch for twelve years and then at Constantinople. He spoke plainly about money, cruelty and the poor. That plain speech, aimed at the court too, led in the end to his exile. He died on the road into a second exile.
entries.teaser: Antioch and Constantinople, 386 to 407 CE. The 'golden-mouthed' preacher who told the rich what they owed the poor, and who died in exile.
entries.longDescription:
John studied rhetoric with Libanius, a famous pagan teacher. He was ordained priest at Antioch in 386. For twelve years he preached there.

In February 398 he was made bishop of Constantinople. The court chose him. It pressed the bishop of Alexandria to make him bishop.

In 403 a synod met at a place called the Oak and condemned him. Two synods had now judged him, and the emperor barred him from his church. Then an imperial decree sent him into exile.

He lived for three years at Cucusus in the mountains. In 407 he was ordered on to Pityus on the Black Sea. He died on the way, on 14 September.
voices: John Chrysostom — the preacher later called 'golden-mouthed', whose sermons, treatises and letters the Library holds
Palladius of Helenopolis — a bishop who stood by him, and wrote a dialogue on his life and fall
entries.legacy: The Reformers read him closely. Calvin quoted him with delight: 'The foundation of our philosophy is humility.' Yet he said Chrysostom gave the human will too much power. In 1530 the Augsburg Confession named him as a witness to how the early church shared Communion.

entries.name: Nestorius
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Moderate. The Library holds three works of his on the shelf of the Antiochene preachers: the Bazaar of Heracleides, his own defense, in English and French, and the fragments of his sermons and letters. The Bazaar survives only in a Syriac translation.
entries.floorNote: Contested. Cyril and the council at Ephesus in 431 judged that his teaching on Christ split him into two. In his own defense Nestorius denied it. Historians still argue over what he really taught; a 1908 study, Nestorius and his Teaching, reopened the question.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within the Antiochene preachers, whose way of speaking about Christ he carried to Constantinople. Cyril of Alexandria wrote against him, and he answered Cyril in his own book. The Church of the East kept that book in Syriac.
entries.why: Nestorius was bishop of Constantinople for three years. He fell in a bitter quarrel with Cyril of Alexandria over how to speak of Christ. He was deposed in 431 and died in exile. His own defense survived in one Syriac copy, kept by the Church of the East. Western scholars found it only in the 1890s.
entries.teaser: Constantinople, 428 to c. 451 CE: a bishop deposed after three years, whose own defense survived only because the Church of the East kept it.
entries.longDescription:
The Library shelves Nestorius's voice with the Antiochene preachers, beside John Chrysostom and Theodore of Mopsuestia. Their story on this map ends in 430. His years as bishop and in exile run past that date.

He became bishop of Constantinople in 428. His sermons soon troubled people. Cyril of Alexandria heard of them and wrote him one letter of warning, then a second.

In 431 a council met at Ephesus. Nestorius would not come before it. The council said he was no longer a bishop. Maximian was made bishop of Constantinople in his place.

Nestorius was sent back to his monastery at Antioch. Later he was banished, and he ended up in Egypt. There, in exile, he wrote his own defense. He called it the Bazaar of Heracleides. In it he names Cyril as his enemy and the cause of his fall. He seems to have written it in 451 or 452, near the end of his life.

His books were ordered burned. The Bazaar survived only in Syriac. The Church of the East kept it, but its opponents called that church Nestorian. In its own synods it gave a different account of its faith.
voices: Nestorius — the deposed bishop of Constantinople, whose own defense, the Bazaar of Heracleides, the Library holds in English and French
Cyril of Alexandria — his chief opponent, whose five books against him the Library also holds
entries.legacy: The Church of the East kept his book. Its Syriac version was made around 535, according to the scholar Bedjan, though the date is not certain. Only one damaged copy was left, in the library of the patriarch of the Church of the East at Kotchanes, in Kurdistan. It was harmed when the Kurdish chief Bedr Khan Bey massacred Christians there in 1843. Western scholars noticed it in the 1890s, and it was printed in 1910.

entries.name: Simeon of Beth Arsham
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Thin but direct. One letter of his survives, on the killing of the Christians of Najran, copied into a Syriac chronicle. John of Ephesus, who inherited some of his letters, wrote his life. One scholar in the 1800s called the letter a forgery, but most accept it as his.
entries.floorNote: The quarrel was over how to speak of Christ after Chalcedon, not over the Nicene Creed.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within the Syriac Orthodox church, the side he fought for inside Persia. He debated the leaders of the Church of the East before a Persian governor. His letter on Najran passed on news from the Christians of Himyar, whose king the Ethiopians had set up.
entries.why: Simeon was a Persian who argued for the Syriac Orthodox faith in the land where the Church of the East was strongest. John of Ephesus called him the Persian Debater. In 524 his letter spread the news of the martyrs of Najran across the Christian world.
entries.teaser: Persia and the Arab camps, c. 497 to 524 CE: a debater who rode to every argument, and whose letter carried the story of the Najran martyrs.
entries.longDescription:
Simeon was a bishop of the Syriac Orthodox side, though he worked inside the Persian empire. John of Ephesus wrote his life. He says Simeon was a Persian, and that he fought the school of Nestorius all his life. Wherever a debate was planned, Simeon would turn up, even from days away.

Once the bishops of the Church of the East called his side to a debate. The judge was a Persian governor. Their leader was the catholicos Babai, who held a synod in 497. Babai told the governor that Simeon's party were the king's enemies. After the debate, his own side made Simeon bishop of Beth Arsham by force.

In 524 he was at the camp of the Arab king Mundhir, with an envoy of the emperor Justin. There he heard of the killing of the Christians of Najran, in Himyar. At Nu'man's camp he met a Christian envoy of the late king of Himyar. He wrote it all down in a letter. He asked that the bishop of Alexandria be told, so that he could ask the king of the Ethiopians to help.

John of Ephesus says Simeon died in Constantinople.
voices: Simeon of Beth Arsham — the Persian Debater, whose letter on the Najran martyrs the Library holds inside a Syriac chronicle
John of Ephesus — the bishop who wrote his life and inherited some of his letters
entries.legacy: His letter outlived him in other men's books. A Syriac chronicle of the 560s copied it, and so did John of Ephesus. A Greek account of the same martyrs drew on it in part. So his letter is one of the main roads by which the story of Najran reached later readers.

entries.name: Peter the Iberian
entries.statusDescription: No tradition here tells his story. What is known of him comes from the Life his disciples wrote about 500, and from their book of his sayings and memories.
entries.sourcing: Moderate, and from one side. The Life of Peter was written about 500 by his own circle and survives in Syriac. The Library holds it in German. His disciple John Rufus wrote down his sayings in the Plerophories, held in French, which also keeps one letter of Peter's own.
entries.floorNote: The quarrel was over Chalcedon's formula, not the Nicene Creed. Peter refused the council of 451 all his life.
entries.relationsSummary: Known only through his own disciples. No tradition here tells his story. He was a prince of Kartli in Georgia. He became bishop near Gaza for those who refused Chalcedon. He helped make Timothy a rival bishop of Alexandria. Clergy from Antioch who refused the council joined him.
entries.why: Peter was a prince of Kartli, sent as a boy hostage to the court at Constantinople. He ran away to be a monk in Palestine. After Chalcedon, the people of Maiuma near Gaza carried him off to be their bishop. He spent the rest of his life leading those who refused the council.
entries.teaser: Gaza and Maiuma, 445 to 488 CE. A Georgian prince who fled the palace to be a monk, and became a bishop for those who refused Chalcedon.
entries.longDescription:
Peter the Iberian is known only through his own disciples. No tradition on this map tells his story. He came from the Christian royal house of Kartli, in Georgia, and he led the monks near Gaza who refused Chalcedon.

His father, the Life says, was Bosmarios, king of the Iberians. As a boy of twelve Peter was sent as a hostage to the court of Theodosius II. He grew up in the palace.

He fled to Palestine with his friend John the Eunuch, and there they took up the monk's life. Peter was made a priest in 445.

After the council of 451, the monks of Palestine turned against their bishop, Juvenal, who had signed it. They chose a monk named Theodosius as their new bishop. The people of Maiuma near Gaza seized Peter and took him to Theodosius. Against his will, Theodosius made him their bishop.

When the emperor Marcian moved against them, Peter went to Egypt. At Alexandria the people carried him off to help make Timothy their bishop. Later he lived near Gaza again. He died on 1 December 488.
voices: Peter the Iberian — the Georgian prince and bishop of Maiuma, whose one surviving letter is kept in his disciple's book
John Rufus — his disciple and successor at Maiuma, who wrote down Peter's memories in the Plerophories
entries.legacy: His disciples kept his memory alive. John Rufus took his place as bishop of Maiuma. He wrote down Peter's stories against Chalcedon. Severus of Antioch became a monk in Peter's house near Gaza, about two years after Peter died. Later, as patriarch, Severus held up Peter's practice as a rule to follow.

Graded Widely Accepted, not Documented, because Moberg reports Halévy's view that the letter is a forgery (Nöldeke and Guidi accept it).
